title: Distance From Equator Calculator: How Far North?
description: Measure your distance from the equator with the Distance From Equator Calculator — New York 4,527 km, Chicago 4,657 km, along your meridian. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, New York is 4,527.1 km from the equator and Chicago 4,656.6 km — a 130 km difference that buys Chicago its extra bite of winter.
quick_answer: The Distance From Equator Calculator measures the surface distance from your point to the equator along your meridian — your latitude, priced in kilometres or miles. Enter a place or coordinates and read the number: the fundamental coordinate of climate, day length and how direct your sunlight ever gets.

body.t: Distance from the equator is the first-order climate dial — this makes it a number you can compare between homes, farms and holiday picks.
Degrees are abstract; 4,527 km is a road trip. Students who convert both ways stop fearing the graticule. Related lines: the
The same distance that sets your seasons' strength — check the swing on the
Latitude-derived features (equator distance) feed climate and agriculture models; this is the transparent version of that feature.
Distance = latitude in radians × Earth's radius: New York's 40.7128° → 0.7106 rad × 6,371 km = 4,527.1 km. One degree of latitude ≈ 111.2 km on the sphere — the rule of thumb the calculator refines.
Buenos Aires (−34.6°) and Los Angeles (34.05°) sit nearly the same distance from the equator in opposite hemispheres — matched climates of light, flipped seasons.

faq: Is it just latitude times a constant?
Very nearly — on a sphere, exactly latitude (radians) × radius. The ellipsoid adds a whisper of variation (110.57–111.69 km per degree); the calculator's sphere value sits honestly between.
Inside or outside the line — does it say?
Yes: the result's framing tells you which side of the line your point sits on (for circles and tropics, poleward versus equatorward; for the meridian, east versus west).
The shortest surface distance to the line — for latitude lines that is the meridian arc; for the prime meridian it is the great-circle route to the nearest point of the meridian.
Does terrain or sea level matter?
No — distances are surface geometry on the reference sphere; mountains do not shorten the way to a latitude line.
Stand on the line and it is: the tropics and circles have real ground you can occupy, and the result honours it.
Sphere-accurate to well under a kilometre for these magnitudes — plenty for education, planning and curiosity; geodesists refine with the ellipsoid.
Signs and hemispheres are handled — a southern point measures to southern lines by the same geometry.
